The laws of logarithms are:

- $\log_{n}\left(a\right)+\log_{n}\left(b\right)=\log_{n}\left(ab\right)$ — the product rule

- $\log_{n}\left(a\right)-\log_{n}\left(b\right)=\log_{n}\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)$ — the quotient rule

- $\log_{n}\left(c^{m}\right)=m\log_{n}\left(c\right)$ — the power rule

Using the quotient rule for logarithms, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}& \log_{5}\left(\frac{\sqrt{x}y^{2}}{z^{4}}\right) \\ &= \log_{5}\left(\sqrt{x}y^{2}\right)-\log_{5}\left(z^{4}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the product rule for logarithms, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}& \log_{5}\left(\sqrt{x}y^{2}\right)-\log_{5}\left(z^{4}\right) \\ &= \log_{5}\left(\sqrt{x}\right)+\log_{5}\left(y^{2}\right)-\log_{5}\left(z^{4}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the power rule for logarithms (a square root is a power of one half), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}& \log_{5}\left(\sqrt{x}\right)+\log_{5}\left(y^{2}\right)-\log_{5}\left(z^{4}\right) \\ &= \frac{1}{2}\log_{5}\left(x\right)+2\log_{5}\left(y\right)-4\log_{5}\left(z\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}& \log_{5}\left(\frac{\sqrt{x}y^{2}}{z^{4}}\right) \\ &= \frac{1}{2}\log_{5}\left(x\right)+2\log_{5}\left(y\right)-4\log_{5}\left(z\right)\end{aligned}
$$

These identities hold for $x,y,z>0$.

The laws of logarithms are:

- $\log_{n}\left(a\right)+\log_{n}\left(b\right)=\log_{n}\left(ab\right)$ — the product rule

- $\log_{n}\left(a\right)-\log_{n}\left(b\right)=\log_{n}\left(\frac{a}{b}\right)$ — the quotient rule

- $\log_{n}\left(c^{m}\right)=m\log_{n}\left(c\right)$ — the power rule

Using the quotient rule for logarithms, we get:

$$
\begin{aligned}& \log\left(\frac{\sqrt{x}y^{3}}{z^{5}}\right) \\ &= \log\left(\sqrt{x}y^{3}\right)-\log\left(z^{5}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the product rule for logarithms, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}& \log\left(\sqrt{x}y^{3}\right)-\log\left(z^{5}\right) \\ &= \log\left(y^{3}\right)+\log\left(\sqrt{x}\right)-\log\left(z^{5}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the power rule for logarithms (a square root is a power of one half), we have

$$
\begin{aligned}& \log\left(y^{3}\right)+\log\left(\sqrt{x}\right)-\log\left(z^{5}\right) \\ &= 3\log\left(y\right)+\frac{1}{2}\log\left(x\right)-5\log\left(z\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}& \log\left(\frac{\sqrt{x}y^{3}}{z^{5}}\right) \\ &= 3\log\left(y\right)+\frac{1}{2}\log\left(x\right)-5\log\left(z\right)\end{aligned}
$$

These identities hold for $x,y,z>0$.

question.:question/problem:
Assume $x>0$.

Express $3\log_{3}\left(2\right)+\log_{3}\left(x\right)-\log_{3}\left(4\right)$ as a single logarithm.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Using the power rule for logarithms, rewrite the powered numerical term and evaluate the power:

$$
\begin{aligned}& 3\log_{3}\left(2\right)+\log_{3}\left(x\right)-\log_{3}\left(4\right) \\ &= \log_{3}\left(2^{3}\right)+\log_{3}\left(x\right)-\log_{3}\left(4\right) \\ &= \log_{3}\left(8\right)+\log_{3}\left(x\right)-\log_{3}\left(4\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the product rule for logarithms, combine the factors with the same sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}& \log_{3}\left(8\right)+\log_{3}\left(x\right)-\log_{3}\left(4\right) \\ &= \log_{3}\left(8x\right)-\log_{3}\left(4\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the quotient rule for logarithms and simplifying the numerical factor, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}& \log_{3}\left(8x\right)-\log_{3}\left(4\right) \\ &= \log_{3}\left(\frac{8x}{4}\right) \\ &= \log_{3}\left(2x\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}& 3\log_{3}\left(2\right)+\log_{3}\left(x\right)-\log_{3}\left(4\right) \\ &= \log_{3}\left(2x\right)\end{aligned}
$$

These identities hold for $x>0$.

question.:question/problem:
Assume $x,y,z>0$.

Express $-2\log_{2}\left(x\right)+\frac{1}{2}\log_{2}\left(z\right)+3\log_{2}\left(y\right)$ as a single logarithm.
question.:question/worked-solution:
First reorder the terms so the two positive logarithms are together:

$$
\begin{aligned}& -2\log_{2}\left(x\right)+\frac{1}{2}\log_{2}\left(z\right)+3\log_{2}\left(y\right) \\ &= \frac{1}{2}\log_{2}\left(z\right)+3\log_{2}\left(y\right)-2\log_{2}\left(x\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Using the power rule for logarithms, we can rewrite the terms as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}& \frac{1}{2}\log_{2}\left(z\right)+3\log_{2}\left(y\right)-2\log_{2}\left(x\right) \\ &= \log_{2}\left(\sqrt{z}\right)+\log_{2}\left(y^{3}\right)-\log_{2}\left(x^{2}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Now, using the product rule for logarithms, we combine the factors with the same sign:

$$
\begin{aligned}& \log_{2}\left(\sqrt{z}\right)+\log_{2}\left(y^{3}\right)-\log_{2}\left(x^{2}\right) \\ &= \log_{2}\left(y^{3}\sqrt{z}\right)-\log_{2}\left(x^{2}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, using the quotient rule for logarithms, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}& \log_{2}\left(y^{3}\sqrt{z}\right)-\log_{2}\left(x^{2}\right) \\ &= \log_{2}\left(\frac{y^{3}\sqrt{z}}{x^{2}}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}& \frac{1}{2}\log_{2}\left(z\right)+3\log_{2}\left(y\right)-2\log_{2}\left(x\right) \\ &= \log_{2}\left(\frac{y^{3}\sqrt{z}}{x^{2}}\right)\end{aligned}
$$

These identities hold for $x,y,z>0$.
